tweet: Interview Q: Your CISO wants centralized security findings across 50+ AWS accounts. SecurityHub is enabled but findings are scattered. How do you aggregate them for executive reporting? #AWS #CloudSecurity
reply: Enable SecurityHub in a dedicated security account as the aggregator. Use cross-account access to collect findings from all member accounts. Set up EventBridge rules for critical findings. Most miss the custom insights feature for exec summaries.

tweet: Interview question I keep hearing: "You've got 50 AWS accounts. How do you manage IAM across all of them without losing your mind?" Most people blank here. #AWS #DevOps
reply: Real answer: AWS Organizations + SCPs for guardrails, then cross-account roles with external IDs. Don't try to manage each account manually — you'll hate yourself in 6 months. #AWS

tweet: Interview question I keep hearing: "Why would you choose Fargate over EC2?" Most people fumble the answer. The real reason? You're paying for compute you actually use, not idle capacity. But there's a catch most miss.
reply: Fargate shines when you have unpredictable, bursty workloads. Cold starts matter less, scaling's instant. BUT if you're running 24/7 steady-state apps, EC2 Reserved Instances destroy Fargate on cost. Know your workload pattern or you'll burn money.

tweet: Your CloudFormation stack fails with a rollback. You didn't enable termination protection. Now all your resources are gone. How do you prevent this from happening again?
reply: Set DeletionPolicy to Retain on critical resources (databases, S3 buckets). Enable stack termination protection before prod deployments. Also: practice stack updates in staging first — rollbacks happen fast.

tweet: Your k8s cluster allows anyone to deploy a container with root. That's not a platform issue—it's a policy issue. Ever heard of OPA? #Kubernetes #DevOps #Security #CloudNative #SRE
reply: OPA (Open Policy Agent) lets you enforce rules before anything hits etcd. Block privileged pods, enforce resource limits, audit image registries. It's admission control that actually scales. #Kubernetes #Policy #InfraAsCode

tweet: Your k8s cluster runs without admission control? You're basically leaving the front door unlocked. What stops someone from deploying a container as root or mounting the host filesystem?
reply: OPA/Gatekeeper lets you enforce policy before anything hits etcd. Deny privileged pods, require resource limits, block certain registries. It's the guardrail between 'it works' and 'it works safely'.

tweet: Your k8s cluster audit logs are sitting in CloudTrail but nobody's actually reading them. How do you know if someone just gave themselves admin access 3 days ago? #Kubernetes #AWS #SecurityAudit #DevOps #CloudTrail
reply: Parse CloudTrail for k8s API calls, filter by user/service account, set up alerts on RBAC changes. Most teams skip this until after an incident. That's the mistake. #Kubernetes #AWS #SecurityAudit #DevOps #SRE

tweet: Your ECS task keeps crashing on deploy but the CloudWatch logs show nothing. Where do you even look first? #AWS #ECS #DevOps #Troubleshooting #CloudComputing
reply: Check the ECS task definition's container logs, but also dig into the agent logs on the EC2 instance itself. Task definition pull failures, IAM role issues, or resource constraints won't always surface in container output. Been there. #AWS #ECS #CICD

tweet: Your CI/CD pipeline deploys every commit straight to prod. GuardDuty flags suspicious API calls from your deployment role. Do you even know what happened? #DevOps #CICD #AWS #SecurityFirst #CloudNative
reply: This is why you need audit logging on IAM. GuardDuty catches the behavior, but CloudTrail tells you WHO triggered it and WHEN. Your pipeline's service account shouldn't have permissions it doesn't use. #AWS #SRE #InfraAsCode

tweet: Your AWS account has 847 findings in SecurityHub. Half are old. How do you decide what actually needs fixing vs what's just noise? #AWS #DevOps #CloudSecurity #SecurityHub #PlatformEngineering
reply: Real answer: severity + exploitability. A critical finding in an internal tool nobody uses beats a medium finding in your API gateway. Also automate suppressions—document WHY you're ignoring something. Future you will thank you. #AWS #SRE #SecurityOps

tweet: If you're managing cloud resources across AWS, GCP, and Azure separately, you're doing it wrong. Crossplane lets you define everything in Kubernetes. Ever actually used it in prod?
reply: Real talk: the learning curve is steep. You're thinking in CRDs and composition functions instead of CloudFormation templates. But once it clicks? Multi-cloud deployments become boring. That's the goal.

tweet: Your Tekton pipeline runs fine locally. Ships to prod. Suddenly tasks are timing out in CI. What's the first thing you check before blaming the cluster? #DevOps #CICD #Kubernetes #PlatformEngineering #CloudNative
reply: Resource requests vs limits. Local = unlimited CPU/memory. Prod = constrained pods getting throttled or OOMkilled. Tekton tasks inherit the namespace defaults. Most people miss this until 2am. #DevOps #Kubernetes #SRE #TechTwitter

tweet: Your service mesh is adding 50ms latency to every request. Do you rip it out or tune it? Most teams pick wrong because they don't understand what they're actually optimizing for. #Kubernetes #ServiceMesh #DevOps #CloudNative #Terraform
reply: The answer: define your SLO first. If you need sub-10ms p99, mesh overhead matters. But if you're chasing observability + security, that latency tax might be worth it. Real talk — measure before you decide. #SRE #Istio #AWS #InfraAsCode

tweet: Your terraform runs fine locally. Ships to prod. AWS SecurityHub starts screaming about unencrypted volumes you never set. What happened? #Terraform #AWS #DevOps #IaC #SecurityHub
reply: Default values. Your provider or module silently set encryption=false. Always explicitly set sensitive attrs even if they match defaults — future you (and auditors) will thank you. #Terraform #AWS #InfraAsCode

tweet: Your team uses Terraform to provision infrastructure but GitOps for deployments. Now you need to sync state between them. Flux watchers don't magically know about your .tfstate changes. How do you keep them honest? #Terraform #GitOps #Kubernetes #DevOps #InfraAsCode
reply: Most miss this: You need a separate reconciliation loop. Terraform outputs → Git commit → Flux picks it up. Or use Terraform Cloud/Enterprise webhooks to trigger Flux refreshes. The state file alone isn't enough. #Terraform #Flux #CICD #PlatformEngineering #SRE

tweet: Interviewer: "What's the difference between EventBridge and SQS? When would you use one over the other?" Most people mix these up — and it costs them the offer. #AWS #DevOps #CloudComputing #InterviewTips #AWSArchitecture
reply: EventBridge = event routing/filtering to multiple targets. SQS = message queue for decoupling. Use EventBridge for event-driven workflows (many targets). Use SQS when you need guaranteed delivery & worker pools. Common miss: thinking they're interchangeable. #AWS #CloudNative

tweet: Interviewer: "What's the difference between CloudFormation and Terraform?" Me internally: oh god they're actually asking this
reply: CF is AWS-only, uses JSON/YAML templates. Terraform is multi-cloud, HCL syntax, way more flexible. Real talk: learn both because you'll definitely use them 🤷

Interviewer: "When would you use DynamoDB vs a relational database?" — literally every AWS interview lol


DynamoDB's your pick when you need crazy scale, fast reads/writes, and don't mind a schema-less vibe. It's NoSQL so no complex joins. Perfect for stuff like user sessions, IoT data, or anything with unpredictable traffic spikes. RDS is better when you've got complex queries, need ACID transactions, or your data's relational (think ecommerce with orders → items → customers). DynamoDB costs more at small scale but destroys RDS at massive throughput. Know your access patterns before picking one.

#AWS #DynamoDB #CloudArchitecture #DevOpsInterview #InterviewTips

Interviewer: "What's the difference between Docker and Podman?" — loads of people think they're basically the same thing


So Docker uses a daemon (background service running as root) that manages containers. Podman? Daemonless. You run containers directly without needing root privileges, which is a big security win. Both use the same image format so switching isn't painful.

Gotcha: Podman's still catching up on some ecosystem stuff. Docker's just more mature and widely used in prod right now. But Podman's definitely gaining traction, especially for rootless deployments.

#Podman #Docker #CloudArchitecture #DevOps #Containerization

Interviewer: "How do you handle encryption keys in the cloud? Should you manage them yourself or use a service like KMS?" — literally every security round


Honestly, manage them yourself and you're asking for trouble. KMS (or similar) handles rotation, access control, and audit logs automatically. You just call it when you need to encrypt/decrypt. Plus if someone gets your app server, they don't have the keys — they're locked in a separate service. That separation is the whole point. Self-managing keys is fine for learning but in prod? Use the service. It's not worth the risk.

#AWS #CloudSecurity #DevOps #KMS #InterviewTips
